core_message: A 1977 probe with less memory than a phone photo is now one light-day away, and engineers still keep it alive.
title: Voyager 1: The 1977 Probe About to Be One Light-Day Away
description:
On 18 November 2026, Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: 25.9 billion kilometres, so far that light needs a full day to get there. It launched in 1977 with about 69 kilobytes of memory, and engineers are still fixing it by radio, most recently after it went silent for two days in October 2026.

This is the story of how it got there: Jupiter's volcanic moon Io, Saturn and Titan, the Pale Blue Dot, the edge of the Sun's bubble, and the repairs made from a day away at the speed of light.

Key points:
- Launched 5 September 1977, 16 days after Voyager 2
- Flew past Jupiter (1979) and Saturn (1980), then left the plane of the planets
- Entered interstellar space on 25 August 2012
- Fixed from Earth in 2024 after a memory chip failed, and its "dead" thrusters revived in 2025
- One light-day from Earth at 06:16 UTC on 18 November 2026

Sources: NASA JPL and NASA Science Voyager mission updates (2024 to 2026), EarthSky, Wikipedia (Voyager 1, CC BY-SA 4.0).

scenes.narration: Was this the end of Voyager 1? To understand why anyone was still listening, we have to go back to 1977.
In the late 1970s, the outer planets lined up in a way that happens only about once every 175 years.

scenes.narration: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune sat on the same side of the Sun. One probe could swing from one to the next.
NASA built two identical spacecraft. Voyager 2 went first, on the twentieth of August 1977.

scenes.narration: Sixteen days later, on the fifth of September, Voyager 1 lifted off from Cape Canaveral on a Titan rocket.
scenes.heading: 5 September 1977

scenes.narration: It was called Voyager 1 because its faster path would get it to Jupiter first.
It weighed 815 kilograms at launch, less than a small car.
scenes.heading: Voyager 1 at launch

scenes.narration: Its computers held about 69 kilobytes of memory in total. A single photo on your phone takes up more.
scenes.heading: All of its computer memory

scenes.narration: Out where it was going, sunlight would be far too weak for solar panels. So it carried three generators that run on the heat of decaying plutonium.

scenes.narration: It was a message for anyone who might find it. The mission itself was planned to last about five years.
Eighteen months later, on the fifth of March 1979, Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter.
scenes.heading: Jupiter, 5 March 1979

scenes.narration: It came within about 349,000 kilometres of the planet's centre, close enough to watch its storms swirl.
Then came the surprise. A navigation engineer, Linda Morabito, spotted a strange plume rising off the edge of the moon Io.
It was a volcano, erupting. The first active volcanoes ever seen anywhere beyond Earth.
Next came Saturn. On the twelfth of November 1980, Voyager 1 swung past its rings and its giant moon, Titan.
scenes.heading: Saturn, 12 November 1980

scenes.narration: Titan was hidden under a thick orange haze. And getting a close look at it came at a price.
scenes.subject: stage

scenes.narration: The path past Titan bent Voyager 1 up and out of the plane of the planets. There would be no more worlds ahead of it.
Voyager 2 went on to Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 1 was headed into the dark.
For nine more years it climbed away from the Sun. Then, on Valentine's Day 1990, it turned around.
The astronomer Carl Sagan had pushed for one last picture: the planets, seen from outside.
From about six billion kilometres away, Earth was a speck smaller than a single pixel, caught in a ray of scattered sunlight.
Sagan later wrote about that speck. That's here. That's home. That's us.
scenes.text: That's here. That's home. That's us.
scenes.author: Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot, 1994

scenes.narration: Soon after, its cameras were switched off for good, to save power for the long road out.
In 1998 it overtook Pioneer 10 to become the most distant human-made object. It has held that title ever since.
scenes.heading: Farther than anything we have built

scenes.narration: The Sun blows out a wind of charged particles. That wind carves a bubble around the planets, called the heliosphere.
In December 2004, Voyager 1 felt that wind suddenly slow down. It had reached the bubble's outer layers.
On the twenty-fifth of August 2012, about 121 times as far from the Sun as Earth is, it crossed the edge.
Voyager 1 became the first human-made object in interstellar space, the space between the stars.
Scientists needed a year to be sure. The proof came from how the gas around it rang after an outburst from the Sun.
scenes.text: The gas rang like a bell

scenes.narration: By then the spacecraft was 35 years old, and it was starting to wear out.
Its plutonium keeps decaying, so its generators lose about four watts of power every year.
Back in 2004, its main roll thrusters had died after two small heaters lost power. Engineers switched to the backups and carried on.
In 2022 it began reporting nonsense about which way it was pointing. The fix was to switch to a different computer.
Then, in November 2023, something worse. Voyager 1 began sending back a repeating pattern of ones and zeros. Gibberish.
Engineers traced it to one chip in the flight data system. It had failed, taking about three percent of the memory with it.
scenes.heading: Memory lost with one failed chip

scenes.narration: Nobody could go and replace it. So they split the code into pieces and moved each one into memory that still worked.
Every test meant sending a command, then waiting almost two days to see what happened.
On the twentieth of April 2024, the answer came back readable. By June, all four of its working instruments were sending science again.
In October 2024, a fault shut down its main radio. It fell back on a backup transmitter that hadn't been used since 1981.
Then, in 2025, the team tried something nobody expected to work. They tried to wake the main roll thrusters.
Its propulsion lead put it simply. These thrusters were considered dead.
scenes.author: Todd Barber, Voyager propulsion lead, NASA JPL, 2025

scenes.narration: They suspected a switch in the heater circuit had flipped the wrong way. On the twentieth of March 2025, they sent the command to flip it back.
When the reply arrived, the heaters were warming up. Thrusters written off for twenty-one years were back.
They needed them. The backup thrusters' fuel lines are clogging, and without roll control Voyager can't keep its antenna pointed at Earth.
In April 2026, to save power, the team turned off an instrument that had run almost nonstop for 49 years.
In September came a move nicknamed the Big Bang: three devices switched off and three lower-power ones switched on, all at the same moment.
It worked. Then, in October, came the silence.
One set of thrusters had dropped offline. The spacecraft's own fault protection swapped in the backups and put the spacecraft into a safe, stable state.
On the twentieth of October, its signal came back. Alone, almost a light-day from home, it had looked after itself.

fallback.narration: On the twentieth of October, its signal came back. Alone, almost a light-day from home, it had looked after itself.

scenes.narration: As its project manager put it, you wait two days before you finally get a response.
scenes.text: You wait two days before you finally get a response.
scenes.author: Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager, NASA JPL, 2026

scenes.narration: Its radio sends with only about twenty watts. By the time that signal reaches Earth, it takes dishes up to 70 metres wide to hear it.
And now it is about to cross a line no machine has ever crossed.
scenes.text: A line no machine has crossed

scenes.narration: Light from the Moon reaches us in about a second. From the Sun, about eight minutes. From Neptune, about four hours.
scenes.heading: How long light takes to reach Earth

scenes.narration: At 06:16 Universal Time on the eighteenth of November 2026, Voyager 1 will be one full light-day from Earth.
That is about 25.9 billion kilometres, or 16.1 billion miles. Light itself needs a whole day to cover it.
scenes.heading: One light-day

scenes.narration: Voyager 1 took 49 years, two months and eleven days to get there, moving at about 61,000 kilometres an hour.
And yet the nearest star is still more than four light-years away. At this speed, it would take about 75,000 years to cover that distance.
scenes.text: About 75,000 years to the nearest star's distance

scenes.narration: Only two of its ten instruments are still running, listening to magnetic fields and waves in the gas between the stars.
Without the Big Bang, another would have been switched off as early as summer 2027. Now the team has bought it a little more time.
One day there won't be enough power left to run anything. The calls will go unanswered for good.
But Voyager 1 won't stop. It will keep falling outward with its golden record, long after the people who built it are gone.
For now, though, a day away at the speed of light, the most distant thing we have ever built still answers when we call.
